title: Western Ancestors, Part 4: Suzuki Roshi
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching is that true fulfillment and peace can be found not by achieving some specific state or goal, but by embracing the present moment and finding courage in the midst of challenges. This sense of "okay-ness" or feeling enough can be a powerful antidote to feelings of inadequacy, and it can be cultivated through the practice of zazen and other spiritual disciplines. By letting go of ego and attachment, we can find freedom and peace, even in the face of difficulties, and discover that true understanding comes from embracing the endless nature of practice.

sentences.text: Good evening everybody.
I was thinking during, I was experiencing and then thinking about my experience a little bit during zazen.
I don't know, can we experience and think about experience at the same time?
Is it like we have an experience and we think about it and then we have another experience?
Or is thinking itself an experience?
I don't know.

But anyway, what I was thinking about was what a blessing it is, stopping, finally really stopping and just being still, taking a sort of deep break from responding to things and fixing things and reacting to things and just resting in our breath and body.
What a blessing the way that can remind us in such a visceral way, a gut way.
It's enough, you know what I mean?
Doesn't it feel like so much of the time it's not enough, we're not enough, nothing's enough, we'll never be enough?
I think that maybe that's one of the great virtues of zazen.
Not that it exactly calms us down or that we figure anything out or that we have great flashes of insight, although that would be nice.
That's okay when that happens, if that happens.
But maybe the great virtue is just this deep felt sense of okay-ness, you know what I mean?
And then even if we plunge into our evening and the next day and forget all about that and are frantic and confused, I think somehow it's like rubbing something.
Like you rub it long enough, you don't forget the feeling of it.
And then I was thinking, once we got to start to do the rest of the ritual of the evening, well, maybe it's not just the meditation.
Maybe it's some kind of immersion in a network or a mesh or a pattern that we do together.
You need other people to do this, a pattern of support, a ritual, life.
So who knows if it's the meditation or the chanting or doing all this with such care.
But somehow it helps, I think.
Somehow it really helps.
And the sense that things are enough and we are enough, this doesn't mean that there aren't problems.
This doesn't mean that we don't have work to do.
So won't we be so much more helpful to ourselves and others and so much more able to appreciate and enjoy our life with its challenges if we can regularly touch into this feeling of, okay?
Do you know what I mean?
Just, okay.
So I thought we'd continue our stories about Zen pioneers, the first people to bring this way of practicing, this matrix of understanding, this vehicle for feeling, this sense that it's enough.
I thought we'd continue with these stories.
That'll be our focus through the practice period, which starts on January 27th, but we're warming up, because there's way more than we could fit in the six weeks of the winter practice period anyway.

I was going to very carefully try to prepare something about Suzuki Roshi, but then I was re-reading Rick Fields' amazing book, How the Swans Came to the Lake, which was the source that I used in Rohatsu sesshin, if you were here, and it'll be on the website to listen to.
I was talking earlier about a Japanese priest named Nyogen Senzaki, who came to America in 1905 or so, 1907 maybe, and lived quietly.

A Japanese ordained Zen priest came with his teacher, and his teacher left him here in this classic moment of Zen drama, which you should listen to the talk or read the book if you don't know about that.
It's an amazing little story.
Oh, I can't resist.
I'll tell you the story.
So Nyogen Senzaki came to America with his teacher, Soyan Shaku, and they'd been invited by a wealthy, liberal, educated family in San Francisco to come and teach Zen, to the household.
So the first ever recorded serious teachings of Zen were given to this couple in this house in San Francisco, mostly to the woman of the family.
I forget her name right now.
I was going to say Mrs.
Russell, but what's her first name?
I can't remember.
And she supposedly is the first Westerner ever to undertake Zen koan studies in her house with this private Zen master.
Anyway, Nyogen Senzaki was a student of Soyan Shaku, and he came with them to help out.
But they didn't present him as a monk or as my assistant.
They presented him, for whatever reason, as a houseboy.

And so Nyogen Senzaki was in his early 20s, worked in this wealthy San Francisco house as a servant, a Japanese servant, and eventually the head housekeeper got tired of him because his English was no good and he was confused.
He wasn't a very good houseboy.
And so they left.
They had to leave eventually.
And so then Nyogen Senzaki and his teacher are walking across Golden Gate Park.
You ever been to Golden Gate Park?
They're walking across some part of Golden Gate Park on a misty day.
And his teacher is carrying his suitcase for him and they're going to go to a hotel.
And his teacher stops moving and sets down the suitcase and says, it's no good for you to just be my assistant.
You need to find your own way.
You should meet this new country of America and see if it beats you or you beat it.
And he set down the suitcase and turned around and walked away.
And Nyogen Senzaki never saw him again in his life.
So anyway, it's an amazing story, all told beautifully in Rick Fields' book.
So then in classic Zen form, he felt like he wasn't ready to try to start teaching Americans about Zen.
And he had to survive somehow.
So he worked in hotels.
He figured his failure as a houseboy meant he should try again with hotels.
And so he spent 17 years working in various positions in hotels until finally he decided maybe he was ready.
And he had enough money to rent a meeting room for the evening.
And he hung up some signs and gave his first Zen talk.
And then he went on like that for the rest of his life, just giving Zen talks when he could.
He eventually lived in Los Angeles and taught out of an apartment.
Died in the late 50s or early 60s or something like that.
So anyway, I was going to write a talk about Suzuki Roshi, but then I look at Rick Fields' chapter and it really is great.
So I'll just read it.
Because this is the next wave.
Yogi and Suzuki, and there are two other known Japanese priests who did similar things in the 20s, 30s, 40s into the 50s.
They were the first wave.
And then starting in the 50s and in the 60s, there was a second wave that had a very different sort of approach.
And conditions in America were very different by then.
*Quote, "Where there is practice, there is enlightenment."
And above all was the message Shunryu Suzuki Roshi brought to America.
Be sure, it's not as simple as it sounds.
And even the most casual glance at Dogen's Shobogenzo will show this.
But it was direct.
It cut everything away that might prevent getting on with the work at hand.
The past, the future, the fear of failure, the hope of success.* [unclear: "Today dream about"] *the wonderful person one will become when enlightened is not true practice, Suzuki taught.
To bemoan the past that has led to one's wretched present is not true practice.
True practice might be big enough to encompass past and future.
But it could only happen in the present moment.
This breath going in, going out, coming in.
Like a swinging door is the Roshi.
Because your breath is like a swinging door in your heart.
So they sat.

The Roshi walked around silently behind them, correcting posture, tilting a chin in, moving a shoulder a little to left or right, adjusting the fingers that formed the mudra, left over right, thumbs barely touching, so that only the thinnest tissue of paper could pass through, just so.
Not too loose, not too tense.*
*The Zen masters of the previous generation, Senzaki and* [unclear: "Sokeyan"]*, had not given the physical posture much attention.
Their students had sat in chairs, and they were older people.
Their bones stiff, their muscles tense, and somehow it never seemed possible that they could sit.
This word sit in italics, that they could sit, imperturbable.
But these youths of the 60s had dropped the old rigidities.
They had practiced yoga, they ate brown rice, they wandered through the woods.
They had done all that, and they suspected, at least the ones who made their way to the Soto Zen mission in San Francisco, that all those trips were not enough.
Or, actually, as they would start to say after a little Zen, too much.
It was all extra.
Just to sit, just to eat, just to sleep, just to work, just to carry water and cut wood, as the old Chinese masters said, that's the miracle.*
And we read about Senzaki, the previous generation, that his meetings were like an hour once a week.
He went to his apartment, he sat on chairs for half an hour.
He gave a little talk, and sometimes a little sweet treat.
And then that was it, no chatting.
That was one of his things.
We read about Senzaki Sensei, no chatting.
He didn't want to be in a sense of silence.
So he didn't start Zen centers or anything like that.
But somehow Suzuki Roshi did.
*Shinya Suzuki flew from Tokyo to San Francisco in May 1959.

A photograph taken at the departure shows him waving happily in the bustling airport, a bouquet of flowers in one hand, a package in the other, wearing his black robe and sandals over white tabi, his face lit by a smile curved like the waxing moon.
He looked completely at home at the international, bare, modern spareness of the departure area and very happy.
Shinya Suzuki was met at San Francisco Airport by the congregation of Sokoji.
For the most part, elderly middle-class Japanese-Americans in neat dark suits and matronly dresses.
Sokoji was founded in 1934 by Hosen Isobe, a Soto Zen missionary who had previously established temples in Korea, Hawaii, and Los Angeles.*
So that's interesting to remember, too, that we read these stories and we're going to talk about all this.
When we focus on these Asian teachers coming to teach Westerners meditation, actually these are religions like any other religion.
And so Japan and the Soto Zen Church have been sending priests to all over the world for a while to serve Japanese immigrants in different parts of the world.
So that's how he got here.
He wasn't heading over to teach the hippies.
He had a job.
He had a gig to run a temple, to be a priest.
*And Shinya Suzuki was the sixth priest to arrive from Soto Zen headquarters in Japan.
The temple, which was designated as a Soto Zen mission, was located in an ordinary wooden building at 1881 Bush Street in that part of San Francisco known as Japantown.
The building, Sephardic, Moorish in design, had a big soaring tower and arabesque-like carvings on the facade.
It had originally been built as a synagogue during the 1890s.

Next door in a smoky windowless room was a neighborhood go club, a kind of unofficial community center for the men who played there every evening until their children came to tell them it was time to come home.*
*Sokoji had nearly been lost during the war when all its members had been interned, but they somehow managed to continue the mortgage payments from the camps.
And when the war was over, the building was still theirs.

For most of its existence, Sokoji, like most of the Asian American Buddhist temples, had remained, in Alan Watts's words, a circumscribed service center for the Japanese community, which, quote, gave no substantial alternative to that that was already being offered in the Presbyterian and Methodist churches.* Not too sympathetic.
*Things began to change with Shinri Suzuki's predecessors.
Hodo Tobasi and his assistant, Katsumitsu Kato.

Tobasi taught some Americans calligraphy, and Kato and Watts himself, teaching them at the American Academy of Asian Studies, shared their love of good cooking and spent hours reading the Rinzai Roku and Bankei together,* famous Zen texts.
*And even before Shinri Suzuki's arrival in San Francisco, a few Americans had begun attending the services at Sokoji.

One of these, a member of the first Zen Institute of America in New York, had read lectures by* [unclear: "Sokeon"]*,* who was a contemporary of Senzaki I was speaking about, but in New York, *to a small group there on Friday nights, a practice which was discontinued when Shinri Suzuki arrived.*
I didn't know that before this.
They had a little Zen study group at Sokoji, Westerners did.
*"We have a new priest," he wrote his friends back east, "who speaks English fairly well and he's a grand person.
Everyone at our temple is more than happy to have him as a teacher.
They sat facing the wall, all lights out except the candle on the altar.
Sensei walks around with a big stick and quite a few get* [unclear: "good wax"]*."*
*There were 12, 12 and 30, 12 to 30 people must mean. 12 to 30 people sitting together on Wednesday nights when the letter was written in 1961.
Several of them, quote, boys that looked like beatniks with beards, sweatshirts and some with sandals.
But I must say, they seemed sincere.
Shunryu Suzuki himself was quoted by a journalist as saying, my first young person was a girl who turned up and said, my husband wants to go to Japan to study Zen.
I replied, instead he should stay here and see.
Why don't you study too?
In any case, within a few years, the number of Americans who came to Sokoji had increased dramatically.
To all of them he said the same thing.
I sit at 5.30 every morning, you are welcome to join me.* It's like one of the most famous Zen expressions: I sit at 5.30 every morning, you're welcome to join me.
*Like most Japanese Zen priests, Shunryu Suzuki was following his father's profession.
His position was, in effect, almost hereditary.
But unlike most priests in his position, Shunryu Suzuki had not become his father's disciple.
He said he left home at the age of 13 to study with Gakuchu So-an Roshi, a disciple of his father and a strict disciplinarian.
Out of five disciples during this period, Shunryu Suzuki was the only one not to leave.*
We can read a lot more about this in the book *Crooked Cucumber*.
Quite a few more details that probably Rick Fields wouldn't know.
What happened really bordered on abuse, we would say.
Very strict.
*At the age of 19, he completed high school, a school connected with Komazawa Buddhist University, and then went on to the university itself.
In his junior year, he boarded with an English woman, Mrs.
Ransom, who had tutored the Crown Prince.
Mrs.
Ransom did not think much of Buddhism and she liked to tease her boarder about his religion.
But by the time he graduated and continued his Buddhist training at Eiheiji, Mrs.
Ransom had become his first student.
It was at that time that Suzuki's desire to go to America and teach first manifested.
So he studied English with her.
He felt, as Richard Baker, one of his closest disciples, later said, that Buddhism needed some fresh opportunity, someplace where people's minds weren't already made up about Buddhism.*
*But Shunryu Suzuki's teacher did not like the idea, and so he asked as a kind of second choice if he could go to Hokkaido, which was in a frontier region only recently settled.

When he was refused there as well, Suzuki settled down in Japan and became a priest at a temple called Zoenji, and then after his teacher died, of Rinzoen, his teacher's temple,* which many of us have been to, Rinzoen.
*During the Second World War, Shunryu Suzuki was conspicuous by his refusal to help the government inspire the populace with the proper samurai spirit.
Instead, he formed a local discussion group to discuss the implications of militarism.
He never spoke much about what happened during the war.*
*He apparently continued to speak out and even published some of his talks.

When the war was over and the occupation army revoked the teaching license of all Zen priests who had actively supported the war, copies of his lectures were accepted as evidence in his favor, and he was able to keep his license to teach high school English.* I guess that's part of what he did to support himself in Japan.

*After the war, Suzuki worked hard to rebuild his country and fulfilled his teacher's wishes by completing the restoration of Rinzoen, a task which took longer than usual since he insisted that everything be done using traditional methods.
He also reestablished two kindergartens.
His first wife died before the war and he married the principal of one of the kindergartens, Mitsu Matsuno.*
*When he accepted a three-year temporary appointment as priest of Sokoji, everyone was surprised.
And after two and a half years in America, his wife and youngest son were sent to bring him back.
But they also stayed.

And when it finally became clear that he would not return, his eldest son, Huichi,* this is Huichi, I think it's actually Huitsu, *replaced him as head of Rinzoen.* And we find out later also that this was not a terribly happy thing for his family.
Nobody's perfect.
*Zazen was the heart of what Shunryu Suzuki taught.

Leg crossed, back straight, chin in, eyes half open, looking down, hands folded, body erect and relaxed, attention on breathing, counting one to ten, sitting like a frog on a lily pad on the round black zafu that Suzuki Roshi had brought from Japan.
At first on benches downstairs and then in the small zendo that he had built upstairs and then, as that became crowded, along the balconies.
This sitting was itself the expression of Buddha nature.
According to the law of Buddha, Suzuki Roshi quoted Dogen Zenji, the patriarch of Soto Zen, body and mind are originally one, essence and form are not two.
In other words, the posture of Zazen itself was not different from the attitude of mind, it proclaimed.
These forms are not the means of obtaining the right state of mind, Suzuki told the students who joined him in the early morning, to take the posture itself is to have the right state of mind.*
*Just sit, nothing to be achieved, no grand vision, no wonderful breakthrough to be pointed out or sought.
In one lecture he talked about a woman who had come to him because she lost her temper with her child.
She wanted to know if sitting Zazen would change that.
Roshi laughed a lot, the student remembered, at the idea that Zazen would change somebody.
He said he was a very lazy boy and now he was a very lazy man.

Quote, so long as your practice is based on a gaining idea, he said, you'll have no time actually to gain your ideal, and moreover you'll be sacrificing the meat of your practice.* So not to have some attitude of trying to get something.
*D.T.
Suzuki, decades later, had made Satori and Zen, big experiences, synonymous.
Shunryu Suzuki now did something similar with practice, practice, an English word that he gave a Buddhist spin.
And yet few people, it must be admitted, felt like Buddha the moment they sat down, or at least like they thought Buddha was supposed to feel.
Not to do anything proved difficult.
There may have been levels of relaxation in counting the breath, there were also levels of boredom, irritation, pain, anxiety.
Like most worthwhile activities, Zazen proved easier to begin than to continue.
And it did not provide much in the way of entertainment.
But then, that was the point.*
*When a fish swims in the water, there is no end, Shunryu Suzuki quoted Dogen again.
And then he went on.
It is very interesting that there is no end.
Because there is no end to our practice, it is good.
Don't you think so?
Usually you expect our practice to be effective enough to put an end to our hard practice.
If I say practice hard for two years, then you will be interested in our practice.
If I say you have to practice your whole lifetime, you will be disappointed.
You will say, oh, Zen is not for me.
If you understand the reason you are interested in this practice is because our practice is endless, that is good understanding.
That is true understanding.
That is why I am interested in Buddhism.
There is no end.*
*Right from the start, it was clear that Shunryu Suzuki was at home in America, and it didn't bother him that the students scarcely knew anything about Buddhism or Zen culture.
This was, in a certain way, an advantage.
As beginners, they had already glimpsed one of the most essential points, what the Japanese call Shoshin, beginner's mind.
Spiritual practice in the West had long been associated with great accomplishment and mysterious power.
But as Suzuki Roshi explained, in the beginner's mind there is no thought, I have attained something.
When we have no thought of achievement, no thought of self, we are true beginners.
It was an inspired move of cross-cultural jujitsu.

By identifying beginner's mind with Zen practice, Shunryu Suzuki reversed in one stroke the inferiority of America so often felt towards the overwhelmingly mysterious and complex traditions of the Orient.
What might have seemed a problem instead became a possibility.
In beginner's mind, as he said, there are many possibilities.
In expert's mind, there are few.*
So it brings a little freshness to it.
*But being open to the creative possibilities of American Buddhism did not make things easier.
Suzuki Roshi lectured in English on traditional difficult texts, the Blue Cliff Record, the Lotus Sutra.
There is sesshin, long day sittings, first on weekends and then in 1962, the first full seven-day sesshin.
Slowly he began to add elements of what he called the rigid formal way of practicing Zen.* The rigid formal way.

*Long established rules govern every move of the Zendo and the observation of these rules cut right across the grain of American individualism, the notion that freedom meant, as Suzuki Roshi said, physical freedom, the freedom of activity.* So that's a mistaken notion.
*It was just this notion, according to the logic of Zen training, that caused suffering.
Quote, it is not a matter of good or bad, convenient or inconvenient, the Roshi explained.
You just do it without question.
That way, your mind is free.
Even when* [unclear: "Ando suggests"], *much to everyone's amazement, that American Zen ought to have more rules than Japanese Zen.
You think 250 precepts for men and 500 for women is awful, and it should be made simpler, he said.* Not sure where he got 500.
*But I think you will have more difficulty in practicing Zazen in America than we do in Japan.
And this kind of difficulty should be continued forever, or we will not have peace in the world.*
Did you catch that?
So the difficulty is good too.
*He declined to say what additional precepts he might have had in mind.
I don't want to disturb your Zazen, he told one student who asked him.
But he did increase the number of bows before service, from three to nine.
When it was suggested that this might discourage some people, he answered, that is true, very true.
I know people we discouraged.
I know we were causing a lot of discouragement for American people when we bowed nine times, when we bowed only three times in Japan.
I know that very well.
So we bowed nine times here in America.*
I wonder how much it was.
Where was his tongue and his cheek when he gave these little teachings?
*So there were rules, etiquette and decorum.
And this did not change for anyone.
If you wanted to sit in the morning, you were there on your zafu by 5.30.
There was freedom, but the freedom was within form.
And Suzuki Roshi explained it in an austere analysis of that generational conflict that obsessed the decade of the 60s.
Older people might understand that the Heart Sutra meant what it said, emptiness is form.
And younger people might understand what it meant when it said, form is emptiness.
But both were necessary.
There was no traffic to speak of at 5.30 in the morning when the students crossed Bush Street to sit at Sokoji.
But they waited at the corner before the* [unclear: "distorted street"] *until the light clicked to green.
And then, only then, did they walk across the white crosswalks.
Something their contemporaries, a few blocks away, in Haight-Ashbury, would never have dreamed of bothering with.*
So we'll have to continue later.
That's the beginning of the story.
These are wonderful stories.
They're only stories.
Who knows what really happened for any one particular person in that time, in that practice.
But somehow, from 1959 when Suzuki arrived in San Francisco, day after day, people have practiced in this way that we practice tonight, and just kept at it.
Do we know why, exactly?
Hard to say.
But somehow it helps.
Not that we're getting any smarter or any wiser or any better.
Maybe we are.
But this quality, I think, of touching some deep-felt sense of who we are, maybe that's what he brought.

At one point Norman, my teacher, our guiding teacher, was talking to his teacher, [unclear: "Soja"] Roshi, and Norman said in a talk, something like, well, what's great about them and about my teacher is that they didn't teach me anything.
They didn't give me anything.
That's what's great.
And apparently Soja didn't really like that that much.
He worked really hard to try to help this young man, Norman Fischer, actually took him in.
And Mel took Norman in when he was sort of lost at sea.
And then later Mel had an opportunity to do calligraphy on a new rakusu, a sort of bib-like thing that we have in our tradition.
You can put an inspiring phrase on there.
And Mel, Sojun Mel Weitsman, wrote on that for Norman, all I can give you is my Zen spirit.
So somehow we received Suzuki Roshi's Zen spirit.
Here we are.
So let's continue.
Attention.
